title: Scrambled Copy Inside a String
statement:
Given two lowercase strings pattern and text, return true if some contiguous piece of text is a rearrangement of pattern: the same letters, each used exactly as many times, in any order.

Otherwise return false. If pattern is longer than text, the answer is false.

examples.why: "bat", starting at index 3, uses t, a and b once each.
t, a and b all appear, but the q splits them. The piece must be contiguous.
"abb" has the same set of letters as "aab", but the wrong counts: one a instead of two. Comparing sets of letters is not enough.

constraints: Both strings hold lowercase English letters only
hints: Two strings are rearrangements of each other exactly when they have the same letter counts. How long must the matching piece of text be?
Every candidate piece has length pattern.length. Moving from one piece to the next adds one letter on the right and removes one on the left.
Keep letter counts for the current window and update them in O(1) per step. To avoid comparing 26 counts each time, also track how many letters currently have the wrong count.

explain.intuition:
A rearrangement has the same letters with the same counts, and the same length as pattern. So only windows of exactly that length matter, and the question for each is "do the counts match?"

Neighbouring windows share all but two letters, so you do not rebuild the counts: add the letter that enters on the right, remove the one that leaves on the left. Comparing two 26-slot arrays per step is already fast. Tracking a single number, how many letters are currently off, makes each step O(1): it changes only when a letter's count crosses its target.
steps: Build diff[c] = (count of c in the first window) − (count of c in pattern), and off = how many letters have diff ≠ 0. If off is 0, return true.

Slide: for each new right end, add its letter and remove the letter that just left on the left. Before changing a letter's diff, if it was 0, increase off; after changing it, if it is now 0, decrease off.
If off reaches 0, return true. If the slide ends without that, return false.
pitfalls: Comparing sets of letters instead of counts: "abb" is not a rearrangement of "aab".
Missing the last window. With pattern "abcd" and text "dcbxabcd", the only match ends at the last character.
Sorting every window. It works, but costs O(m log m) per window, which is far too slow when the pattern is long.

solutions.title: Sort every window
solutions.idea: Sort the pattern once. For each window of the same length, sort it and compare.

solutions.title: Sliding counts, compare 26 slots
solutions.idea: Keep the window's letter counts up to date in O(1) per step and compare them with the pattern's counts.

solutions.title: Sliding counts with an 'off' counter
solutions.idea: Track how many letters currently have the wrong count. Each step changes two letters, so the counter updates in O(1).

followups: Return the start index of every matching window, not just whether one exists.
The strings can hold any Unicode characters. What do you use instead of a 26-slot array?
